newsitem.title: UK: Bass welcome proposals on drink laws.
newsitem.headline: Bass welcome proposals on drink laws.

text.p: Brewing-to-leisure group Bass Plc said on Thursday it welcomed government proposals aimed at curbing alcohol consumption by under-age drinkers.
The proposals include a "number of sensible and decisive actions which Bass Brewers welcomes", a company spokesman told Reuters.

Hoopers Hooch, brewed by Bass, is the nations most popular so-called "alcopop" -- alcoholic lemonades and sodas. The marketing of alcopops has been heavily criticised by government for appealing to under-age drinkers.
"The only way to address under-age drinking is to stop the sale of alcohol to under 18s. A fact which the government has acknowledged in this announcement," said the spokesman.

"By promoting proof of age cards and making it illegal to buy alcohol for under 18s the government has acted positively and focused on the supply of alcohol rather than simply targeting the legal production of legitimate drinks," he added.

There were fears in the brewing and retail industry that the government would ban alcopops outright, but instead the measures are aimed at preventing youngsters from getting their hands on the drinks.
Earlier the government proposed making it an offence for adults to buy alcohol for a juvenile and allowing police to confiscate alcohol from those under-18 drinking in public.
It also proposed using teenagers, working under the close supervision of the police, to check rogue retailers selling alcohol to under-18s.
The drinks have proved a runaway success for the industry. Sales now exceed 250 million pounds a year and it is now the fastest growing sector in the drinks industry.
Other alcopop brands include Two Dogs made by Merrydown Plc and Whitbread Plc's Vanilla Heist and Lemon Jag. Supermarkets also now have their own label brands like Sainsbury's Piranha.
